title: Fraction to Recurring Decimal

blocks.text: Given two integers numerator and denominator representing a fraction, return the fraction as a string. If the decimal part repeats forever, wrap only the repeating portion in parentheses.

blocks.title: Analogy: Long Division on Paper, Watching for a Repeat
blocks.text: This is ordinary long division, carried out one digit at a time, exactly as it is done by hand. The one extra thing to watch for is a remainder that has already shown up earlier in the division, since a repeated remainder means every digit from that point onward is guaranteed to repeat forever in exactly the same pattern.

blocks.caption: Do long division digit by digit, watching for a remainder that repeats

blocks.text: 1 divided by 2 is "0.5", the division ends evenly.
2 divided by 1 is simply "2", a whole number with no decimal part at all.
4 divided by 333 produces the digits 0, 1, 2 forever, giving "0.(012)", with the entire repeating block wrapped in parentheses.
The long division itself is mechanical, the real question worth pausing on is exactly how to efficiently detect that a remainder has shown up before.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Doing long division one digit at a time is the easy part, the genuine difficulty is deciding, as efficiently as possible, whether the current remainder has already appeared earlier in this same division.

Observation 2: Scanning back through every previously seen remainder at each step is a linear search repeated over and over, the exact same shape of inefficiency already solved with a hash set for Happy Number's cycle detection.

Observation 3: Unlike Happy Number, which only needed to know whether a value had been seen before, this problem also needs to know exactly where in the output that remainder's digit was produced, since that position is exactly where the opening parenthesis belongs.

Observation 4: Testing 4 divided by 333 confirms it, storing each remainder's digit position the first time it appears, then checking a hash map directly for every new remainder, replaces the linear scan with a single direct lookup at every step.
That extra requirement, remembering WHERE a value was first seen, not just whether it was seen, is what turns a plain Happy-Number-style hash set into a hash map here.

Perform long division one digit at a time, and after each step, scan back through every remainder seen so far to check whether the current remainder has already appeared. If it has, the repeating part starts exactly where that earlier remainder was seen.

items: Handle the sign, and compute the whole number part and the first remainder directly.
If the remainder is already zero, return the whole number part with no decimal point.
Otherwise, repeatedly multiply the remainder by 10, take the next digit, and update the remainder.
After each new remainder, scan back through every remainder produced so far to see if it repeats.
If a repeat is found, wrap everything from that earlier position to the end in parentheses and stop.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: scan back through every previous remainder after each new digit

codes.python:
def fraction_to_decimal(numerator, denominator):
    if numerator == 0:
        return "0"
    sign = "-" if (numerator < 0) != (denominator < 0) else ""
    numerator, denominator = abs(numerator), abs(denominator)
    integer_part = numerator // denominator
    remainder = numerator % denominator
    if remainder == 0:
        return sign + str(integer_part)                  # the division ends evenly, no decimal needed
    digits = []
    seen_remainders = []                                # every remainder seen so far, in the order seen
    while remainder != 0:
        position = -1
        for idx, seen in enumerate(seen_remainders):       # scan back through every remainder seen before
            if seen == remainder:
                position = idx
                break
        if position != -1:
            digits.insert(position, "(")                    # the repeating part starts right here
            digits.append(")")
            break
        seen_remainders.append(remainder)
        remainder *= 10
        digits.append(str(remainder // denominator))
        remainder %= denominator
    return sign + str(integer_part) + "." + "".join(digits)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    numerator, denominator = 4, 333
    print(fraction_to_decimal(numerator, denominator))

blocks.text: This is correct, since the division is carried out exactly as it would be done by hand, and a repeated remainder genuinely does guarantee the digits from that point will repeat forever.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), where n is the number of decimal digits produced, since every new remainder is compared against every remainder seen before it.
Space: O(n), for the list of remainders and digits.

Limitation: scanning back through every previous remainder, one at a time, repeats a check that could instead be answered instantly. Since only the exact remainder value matters, and not its neighbors, storing each remainder in a hash map alongside the digit position it first appeared at turns that scan into a single direct lookup.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the linear scan works but is wasteful: at every single step it re-checks every remainder ever seen before, even though only an exact match matters, never a partial or nearby one.

What stays the same as Happy Number: the underlying "have I seen this exact value before" question, and the insight that a hash based structure answers that question in constant time instead of linear time.

What is different here: the map must store WHERE each remainder's digit was produced, not just whether the remainder was seen, since that position is exactly where the opening parenthesis needs to go.

Can a plain hash map answer both questions, has it been seen, and where, at once: yes, mapping remainder to digit position serves both purposes with a single data structure and a single lookup.

The core idea: keep a hash map from remainder value to digit position; check it directly instead of scanning, and use the stored position to know exactly where to open the repeating group.

Keep a hash map from a remainder value to the digit position where it first appeared. After computing each new remainder, check the map directly instead of scanning a list. If the remainder is already a key in the map, the repeating part begins at the position stored there.
Keep a hash map from each remainder to the digit position where it first appeared, checking it directly instead of scanning a list at every step.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: look up each remainder directly in a hash map instead of scanning

codes.python:
def fraction_to_decimal(numerator, denominator):
    if numerator == 0:
        return "0"
    sign = "-" if (numerator < 0) != (denominator < 0) else ""
    numerator, denominator = abs(numerator), abs(denominator)
    integer_part = numerator // denominator
    remainder = numerator % denominator
    if remainder == 0:
        return sign + str(integer_part)                  # the division ends evenly, no decimal needed
    digits = []
    seen = {}                                           # maps a remainder to where its digit first appeared
    while remainder != 0:
        if remainder in seen:
            position = seen[remainder]                      # this remainder has shown up before, right here
            digits.insert(position, "(")
            digits.append(")")
            break
        seen[remainder] = len(digits)
        remainder *= 10
        digits.append(str(remainder // denominator))
        remainder %= denominator
    return sign + str(integer_part) + "." + "".join(digits)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    numerator, denominator = 4, 333
    print(fraction_to_decimal(numerator, denominator))

blocks.text: This works because a hash map answers "has this exact remainder been seen, and if so, at what position" in one constant time operation, exactly the two pieces of information the brute force scan was recomputing from scratch at every single step. Since a remainder can only ever repeat an earlier remainder exactly, never approximately, an exact key lookup is both sufficient and correct for detecting the repeat.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a genuine complexity class improvement, every remainder is checked with a single direct lookup instead of a scan.
Space: O(n), for the hash map, this is the real floor for this problem, since every distinct remainder that appears must be remembered somewhere to ever detect a repeat.

blocks.text: This problem is a direct application of the "have I seen this before" pattern, the same idea behind detecting a cycle in general, just applied to the remainders produced during long division rather than to array values or list nodes. A hash map turns a linear scan through history into a single direct lookup, which is exactly what changes the complexity class here.

items: Forgetting to handle the sign correctly, especially when only one of the numerator or denominator is negative.
Not special casing a numerator of zero, which should return "0" directly rather than running through the division logic.
Inserting the opening parenthesis at the wrong position, it must go exactly where the repeating remainder was first seen, not at the very start of the decimal part.

blocks.text: Explicitly naming this as a cycle detection problem in disguise, spotting a repeated remainder during long division, is a strong way to connect it to a much more general pattern rather than treating it as a one off simulation problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid scanning the whole history each time", think: a hash map turns that repeated scan into a single direct lookup.
If the interviewer says "how is this related to Happy Number", think: same "have I seen this before" cycle detection, but the map must also remember where, not just whether.
If the interviewer says "where exactly does the repeating block start", think: exactly at the digit position stored for that remainder the first time it was seen.

items: Why must the map here store a position, while Happy Number's cycle detection only needed a plain set?

Can you determine the maximum possible length of the repeating block without simulating the whole division first?
How would this approach change if you needed to detect repeats in a different positional base than 10?
How would you adapt this to support fractions given as arbitrary precision numbers instead of fixed width integers?

Any long division or repeated-state simulation problem, where the set of possible states is finite and a repeat is therefore mathematically guaranteed eventually.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The linear scan approach runs in O(n squared) time and O(n) space, where n is the number of decimal digits produced. The hash map approach runs in O(n) time, a genuine complexity class improvement, using the same O(n) space, the real floor for this problem.

items: Pattern: "have I seen this before" cycle detection using a hash map, applied to the remainders produced during long division rather than to array values or list nodes.

Core Idea: a hash map from remainder value to digit position replaces a linear scan through history with a single direct lookup, and doubles as the answer to both "has this remainder repeated" and "where does the repeating block begin".
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized version, where n is the number of decimal digits produced.
Space: O(n) for both versions, to hold the remainders or the hash map.
Most Important Observation: a repeat detection problem that also needs to know WHERE a value was first seen calls for a hash map, not just a hash set.
Interview Difficulty: easy to write the long division simulation; recognizing this as a cycle detection problem and reaching for a hash map is what shows real understanding.
One line memory trick: map each remainder to the digit position where it first appeared, check the map instead of scanning history.
